explanation.text: The ending closes what the beginning opened. If the first sentence left a question, the last one answers it, or says why it stays open.
An ending does not tell the story again. It gives the reader one last thought to take away.
The first sentence of an essay makes a reader want to go on. It says what the essay is about, and it leaves a question that only the essay can answer.
Before your next essay, write three first sentences, and keep the one that leaves a question.
A first draft is never the last. Read it again, aloud if you can, and listen for the words that come again and again.
Then change one thing at a time. Say what a repeated word means each time, and use that. Join short sentences that say one thing about the same moment.

demo.text: Read the draft aloud. "Nice" comes three times, and "the robot" begins two sentences.
Say what "nice" means each time. The robot was kind, and the cake was sweet.
Join the sentences that tell one moment: "The kind robot made a sweet cake."
Read it aloud again. Each word now says something new, and nothing is lost from the draft.

statement.text: Make this draft clearer, with fewer repeated words: "The robot was nice. The robot made a nice cake. The cake was nice."

explanation.text: A paragraph holds the sentences about one idea. When the essay moves on, to a new place, a new time or a new idea, a new paragraph begins.
Start each paragraph on a new line, a little way in from the edge, so that the reader sees where it begins.
A short essay has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning says what the essay is about, the middle tells it, and the end closes it.

Read this one, and find where each part begins: "Our street floods every spring. The water comes up to the second step, and we carry the chairs upstairs. Then it goes, and the street smells of the river for a week. I have stopped minding it: spring is when our street remembers it was a river once."

criteria.text: It tells of one day, in paragraphs, in the order things happened.
Its ending says why the day is remembered.
It tells of at least one person or place of that day.

statement.text: Write a short essay about a day of your life that you remember well.
Do not write your name or the real name of anyone you know.

check.key: The door was open, and nobody had opened it.

trap_values.text: Could this sentence open any story at all? Look for one that makes you ask a question.
trap_values.value: It was a day like any other.
I am going to write about a day.

options: It was a day like any other.
The door was open, and nobody had opened it.
I am going to write about a day.

solution.text: "The door was open, and nobody had opened it" leaves a question that only the story can answer: who opened it? The other two sentences give the reader nothing to wait for.

statement.text: Which first sentence makes a reader want to go on?

check.key: At midnight the lighthouse went dark, and a ship was still coming.

trap_values.text: This sentence tells what the essay is about, but nothing has happened yet. Look for one where the story has already begun.
trap_values.value: This essay is about a lighthouse on a rock.

trap_values.text: After this sentence, is there anything left for the reader to find out? Look for one that keeps the end back.
trap_values.value: The lighthouse went out one night, the keeper climbed up and lit it again, and the ship got home safely.

options: This essay is about a lighthouse on a rock.
At midnight the lighthouse went dark, and a ship was still coming.
The lighthouse went out one night, the keeper climbed up and lit it again, and the ship got home safely.

solution.text: "At midnight the lighthouse went dark, and a ship was still coming" starts where something is happening and leaves a question: will the ship be safe? The first sentence only names the topic, and the third tells the whole story, so the reader has nothing to wait for.

statement.text: An essay tells of a lighthouse on a rock in the sea. Which first sentence makes a reader want to go on?

check.key: In our town the snow never stops, and this morning it did.

trap_values.text: This sentence is true of almost any snowy place. What does it make you want to ask? Look for one that makes you wonder.
trap_values.value: Snow is cold and white, and it falls on our town.

trap_values.text: This sentence already tells how the story ends. Look for one that keeps the end back.
trap_values.value: In our town the snow never stops, but one morning it did, the sun melted it all, and we had our first summer.

options: Snow is cold and white, and it falls on our town.
In our town the snow never stops, and this morning it did.
In our town the snow never stops, but one morning it did, the sun melted it all, and we had our first summer.

solution.text: "In our town the snow never stops, and this morning it did" tells something strange and leaves a question: why did it stop, and what happens now? The first sentence could open any story about snow, and the third tells the whole story at once.

statement.text: An essay tells of a town where the snow never stops. Which first sentence makes a reader want to go on?

criteria.text: It tells what the draft tells, in the same order.
The words that the draft repeats most, such as "dragon" and "very", come less often.
Sentences that say one thing about the same moment are joined into one.

statement.text: Here is the draft of a short essay. Write it again on the sheet, so that it is clearer and repeats fewer words.

"The dragon was very big. The dragon lived in a very big cave. Every day the dragon went out of the cave and the dragon flew over the hills. The dragon was very happy when the dragon flew over the hills."
Do not write your name or the real name of anyone you know.

criteria.text: There are three different first sentences, and each could begin an essay about the talking umbrella.
At least one of them leaves a question that only the essay could answer.
The sentence with the ring round it is one that makes a reader want to go on.

statement.text: In a small shop there is an umbrella that can talk, but only when it rains. Write three different first sentences for an essay about it. Then put a ring round the one you would keep.
Do not write your name or the real name of anyone you know.

criteria.text: It is written in paragraphs, each about one part of the morning.
Its ending closes the story of the first morning.
It tells what can be seen, heard or felt on the island.

statement.text: Imagine an island that nobody has found yet. Write a short essay about your first morning there.
Do not write your name or the real name of anyone you know.

criteria.text: Each paragraph is about one part of the day.
A new paragraph begins when the essay moves on to the next part of the day.
It tells of at least one kind of weather that the shop sells.

statement.text: Imagine a shop that sells the weather: a jar of sunshine, a box of fog, a bag of wind. Write a short essay about one day in that shop. Give the morning, the middle of the day and the evening a paragraph each.
Do not write your name or the real name of anyone you know.

read-it-aloud.description: Read the essay aloud: where you stumble, the reader will too.
read-it-aloud.title: Read it aloud

start-in-the-middle.description: Begin where something is already happening, and let the reader catch up.
start-in-the-middle.title: Start in the middle

announcing-the-topic.description: Chose a first sentence that says what the text is about instead of beginning it.
announcing-the-topic.trap_advice: Start where something happens: the reader learns the topic on the way.

flat-opening.description: Chose a first sentence that could open any story, and so promises nothing.
flat-opening.trap_advice: Ask what a reader wants to know after the first sentence: if nothing, it opens no story.

giving-it-all-away.description: Chose a first sentence that tells the whole story at once, and so leaves the reader nothing to find out.
giving-it-all-away.trap_advice: Keep something back: a first sentence opens a question and lets the essay answer it.
